Copper Catalyzed Protosilylation/Protoborylation of gem-
Difluoroallenes
Cui-Cui Shan,
[a]
Kai-Yang Dai,
[a]
Meng Zhao,
[a]
and Yun-He Xu*
[a]
We have developed a protocol for protoborylation and
protosilylation of gem-difluoroallenes to afford gem-difluoroall-
yl-boronates and gem-difluoroallylsilanes. It is different from
non-fluorine allenes in which nucleophiles are added to γ-
position of gem-difluoroallenes to afford β,γ-addition products.
Not only monosubstituted gem-difluoroallenes but also disub-
stituted gem-difluoroallenes could react well with silaboronate
(PhMe
2
Si � Bpin) and bis(pinacolato)diboron (B
2
pin
2
). The proto-
col is simple and efficient to construct compounds which
contain tertiary/secondary gem-difluoroallylboronates and gem-
difluoroallylsilanes. Moreover, diverse organofluorine com-
pounds can be converted from these organoboronates and
silanes.
In the past few decades, allenes have been shown to
demonstrate nice reactivity and selectivity.
[1]
It can usually be
tuned by the electronic or steric effects of its special structure
and the nature of the catalysts in reaction conditions. In view of
the practicability of these approaches, addition reactions
between allene and PhMe
2
Si � Bpin or B
2
pin
2
are investigated in
some reviews.
[2,3]
The different reaction sites of nucleophilic
addition between non-fluorine allene and gem-difluoroallene
by copper catalyst are shown in Scheme 1. Organocopper
compounds are added across the terminal double bond of the
non-fluorine allene to generate a vinylcopper species, which
then reacts with various electrophiles to afford the desired
products
[4,5]
(Scheme 1a). Besides, the nucleophiles added to the
β-position of non-fluorine allene generates allylcopper species
(Scheme 1b and Scheme 1c). The intermediates react with
electrophiles to afford two kinds of β-addition products.
[4,5b,6–15]
Substituted gem-difluoroallenes are designed to prepare
fluorine-containing organic compounds. It is well known that
the fluorine-containing organoboron and organosilicon com-
pounds are attractive synthons that have great potentials for
the construction of diverse organofluorine compounds.
[16]
Unlike non-fluorine allene, the organocopper species normally
attack the α-position of substituted gem-difluoroallenes and
yield the monofluoroallene conpounds. Based on the reaction
pathway, Hammond and collaborators have reported an article
involving the reaction of gem-difluoroallene with Grignard
reagents
[17]
(Scheme 1d). The difluoroallene underwent an
addition-elimination process to yield a trisubstituted mono-
fluoroallene. Besides α-addition, nucleophilic addition of an
organocopper species at the γ-position of substituted 1,1-
difluoroallenes gave 2,2-difluorovinylmetal intermediates. Cap-
turing of these intermediates by electrophiles (E-X) would
provide the desired difluoroalkenes. The gem-difluoroalkenes
bore newly introduced substituent on the γ-C (Nu) position
(Scheme 1e). In 2012, Ichikawa group reported a method for γ-
selective addition to 1,1-difluoroallenes using organocopper
reagents.
[18]
A catalytic amount of CuBr·SMe
2
was not effective
in their reaction and the substrates were not well tolerated
because Grignard reagents were added. In 2020, the same
group reported Au catalyzed α- and γ-addition to gem-

To demonstrate the scalability of our method, we inves-
tigated a gram-scale synthesis of gem-difluoroallylboronate 4 a
and gem-difluoroallyl silicon 5 a. When 1 a was carried out on a
6.0-mmol scale, 4 a and 5 a were obtained in 86 % and 90 %
yields (Scheme 2, eqs 1–2). As shown in Scheme 2, further
derivatization of 4 a and 5 a has been conducted. When the
gem-difluoroallylboronate 4 a was subjected to a homologation
with a halomethyl lithium reagent (Scheme 2, eq 3), the
reaction afforded homoallylboronate 9 and oxygen migration
product 10 in 31 % and 28 % yields. When NaH (3 equiv) was
added to the solution of 5 a in DMSO, the product 11 was
obtained through allyl protonation process in 80 % yield (Z/E =
34 : 66) (Scheme 2, eq 4). Then we tried the reaction of gem-
difluoroallylboronate 4 i with benzaldehyde (Scheme 2, eq 5),
resulting in 70 % yield (E/Z > 95 : 5, dr = 60 : 40) of product 12.
Based on these observations, a plausible mechanism for the
addition of gem-difluoroallene is proposed as illustrated in
Scheme 3. The catalytic cycle is initiated by formation of I from
CuI and Y � Bpin. When Y = Bpin, a boryl copper species
[Cu] � Bpin is generated from the reaction between a copper

In conclusion, we have developed a protocol of copper-
catalyzed boryl- and silyl-addition to gem-difluoroallenes, which
provides access to gem-difluoroalkene compounds. The process
utilizes a commercially available copper catalyst and tolerates a
range of allenes. For borylation process, we attempted different
kinds of diboronate reagents. For silylation process,
PhMe
2
Si � Bpin was used. Corresponding tertiary or secondary
gem-difluoroallylboronates and gem-difluoroallylsilanes were
obtained regioselectivities.
